systems.name: check
systems.title: Simulation oracles
systems.purpose: Holds oracles every simulation needs: a linearizability checker over client histories, a key-value model for it, and a history recorder that understands operations with unknown outcomes (timeouts).
systems.what:
Protocol-specific invariants (one leader per term, identical logs) belong in the test that knows the protocol (dsttest's Always and Final).

hist := check.NewHistory[check.KVInput, check.KVOutput](w) call := hist.Invoke(client, check.KVInput{Op: check.KVPut, Key: "k", Value: v}) if err := put(...); err == nil { call.Return(check.KVOutput{}) } else if definitelyNotApplied(err) { call.Fail() } else { call.Abandon() } ... h.Final("linearizable", func(*dst.World) error { return check.Linearizable(check.KVModel(), hist.Ops(), check.Options{}).Err() })

systems.name: check.Linearizable
systems.title: Linearizability checker
systems.purpose: Decides whether a history matches a sequential model, within a step budget.
systems.what: `Linearizable` splits the history by the model's `Partition`, searches each partition for a real-time-respecting order that the model accepts, and combines the verdicts into one `Result`. The search is bounded in steps, not wall time, and reports Inconclusive when the bound is hit. On a violation it explains the longest order found and the operation it could not place.
systems.doc:
Linearizable checks whether history is linearizable with respect to the model: whether there is a total order of its operations that respects real time and in which each operation's output is what the model produces.

a precedes b in real time when a.Return < b.Call. Operations whose intervals touch or overlap may be ordered either way. An Unknown operation has no return, so it may be placed anywhere after its call, including after every other operation, which is how "it never happened" is expressed.

The search is the Wing & Gong algorithm with Lowe's memoization of (linearized set, state) pairs, the same one Knossos and porcupine use. It is exponential in the worst case, so partition the model where the object allows it.

interface.name: Linearizable
interface.signature: func Linearizable[S comparable, I, O any](m Model[S, I, O], history []Op[I, O], opts Options) Result
interface.doc: Checks a history against a model; returns a Result.

laws.text: On every history it decides within budget, its verdict equals that of trying every order of the operations.
Any history from running the operations one at a time, each inside its interval, is linearizable.
With a Partition function, the verdict is Pass exactly when every partition alone is.
The same history and options always give the same Result, Steps included.
Result.Err is nil exactly for Pass and wraps ErrInconclusive exactly for Inconclusive.
A Violation in any partition wins over Inconclusive in others.
laws.detail: Partitions are checked in sorted key order; the first violating partition is reported, else the first inconclusive one.

laws.text: Operations whose intervals merely touch may be ordered either way.
laws.detail: At equal times calls sort before returns, so a.Return == b.Call does not force a before b.

laws.text: MaxSteps bounds each partition separately; zero means 10 million.
laws.detail: Result.Steps is the total across partitions checked.

laws.text: An empty history, or empty partition, passes.
A Violation's Explanation names the operation that could not be placed.

assumes.text: Model.Step is pure and returns legal=true when known is false.
assumes.detail: The search memoizes (linearized set, state) and backtracks by restoring saved states.

assumes.text: Model states compare equal with == exactly when they are the same state.

systems.name: check.Model
systems.title: Sequential model
systems.purpose: Describes the sequential object a concurrent history must be equivalent to.
systems.what: A `Model` is a set of functions: `Init` for the starting state, `Step` to apply one operation and judge its output, an optional `Partition` to split histories into independent parts, and an optional `Describe` for reports. `Op` is the history entry the checker consumes. The model owns the object's semantics; the search is left to `Linearizable`.

interface.name: Model
interface.doc: Init, Step, optional Partition and Describe for an object.

interface.name: Op
interface.doc: Client, input, output, call/return times, Unknown flag.

laws.text: Without Partition, the whole history is one partition and Result.Partition is empty.
Without Describe, reports render operations with %v, and unknown outputs as ?.
An Unknown op's Return time is ignored by the checker.

systems.name: check.History
systems.title: History recorder
systems.purpose: Records client operations and their endings for Linearizable, timed by a World.
systems.what: `History` collects one `Op` per `Invoke`, and each returned `Call` is ended by `Return`, `Fail` or `Abandon`. Times are durations since the history was created, read from the World's clock. `Ops` produces the slice `Linearizable` consumes, leaving failed operations out and marking unfinished ones Unknown.
systems.doc:
History records client operations for Linearizable, with times from a World's clock. It is safe for concurrent use (the real World's clients run in parallel).

Each operation ends in one of three ways: - Return: the client saw the result. The output is known. - Fail: the client learned that it definitely did not happen (for example "not the leader, nothing was proposed"). It is left out of the history. - Abandon (a timeout), or no ending before the run ends: the outcome is unknown. It may still take effect later.

The first ending counts. A reply that arrives after Abandon is ignored, because the client has stopped waiting for it.

interface.name: NewHistory
interface.doc: Empty history timed by the World's clock.

interface.name: History.Invoke
interface.signature: func (h *History[I, O]) Invoke(client int, in I) Call[I, O]
interface.doc: Records an invocation now and returns its Call.

interface.name: Call.Return
interface.signature: func (c Call[I, O]) Return(out O) bool
interface.doc: Records completion with output; reports if first ending.

interface.name: Call.Fail
interface.doc: Records the operation definitely did not happen.

interface.name: Call.Abandon
interface.doc: Records an unknown outcome; later replies ignored.

interface.name: History.Ops
interface.doc: Returned and unknown operations, failed ones dropped.

interface.name: History.Len
interface.doc: Number of operations invoked, including failed ones.

laws.text: Only the first Return, Fail or Abandon of an operation affects Ops.
An operation that was invoked and never returned or failed appears in Ops with Unknown set.
A failed operation doesn't appear in Ops.
Call and return times come from the World's clock, so they are simulated times in a simulation.
Return, Fail and Abandon report true only for an operation's first ending.
Ops lists operations in Invoke order.
Call and Return times are measured from when NewHistory was called.
Len counts every Invoke, failed operations included.

systems.name: check.KVModel
systems.title: Key-value model
systems.purpose: Ready-made Model of a string map with get, put and delete.
systems.what: `KVModel` returns a `Model` whose state is one key's value and presence, partitioned by key so each key is checked on its own. Inputs are `KVInput` (op, key, value) and outputs `KVOutput` (value, found). It relies on callers giving every put a unique value so stale reads are distinguishable.
systems.doc:
KVModel is a linearizable map from string keys to string values, with get, put and delete. It partitions by key, so each key is checked on its own.

Give every put a unique value. A checker can only catch a stale read if it can tell the two values apart.

interface.name: KVModel
interface.doc: Model for a string-keyed map partitioned by key.

laws.text: A get returns the latest put's value on its key, or not- found if none or deleted since.
laws.detail: Puts and deletes accept any output.

laws.text: A get with an unknown outcome changes nothing and is always legal.
Operations on different keys never constrain each other.
An input whose Op is not get, put or delete is always illegal.
A put or delete with unknown outcome may still take effect.
laws.detail: Step applies the state change regardless of known.

laws.text: Reports mark operations with unknown outcome with ?.

systems.name: dst
systems.title: World API
systems.purpose: Is what code uses, instead of the language and the standard library, for everything that waits or is nondeterministic: goroutines, channels, select, sleeping, the clock, timers, locks, contexts, randomness, files and the network.
systems.what:
A World provides them.

In production the World is real (package realworld): every operation is the plain Go one. In tests the World is simulated (package dsttest): one seed decides every goroutine interleaving, delay and fault, so a failing seed replays exactly.

Migrating code is a mechanical substitution:

go f()                  w.Go(f) make(chan T, n)         dst.MakeChan[T](w, n) c <- v / <-c / close    c.Send(v) / c.Recv() / c.Close() for v := range c        for v := range c.All() select { ... }          dst.Select(w, dst.OnRecv(c, ...), dst.OnSend(...), dst.Default(...)) time.Now / Sleep        w.Now() / w.Sleep(d) time.NewTimer/After     w.NewTimer(d) / w.After(d) sync.Mutex/WaitGroup    dst.Mutex / dst.WaitGroup (zero values work) context.WithTimeout     dst.WithTimeout(w, ctx, d) math/rand, crypto/rand  w.Rand() os, net                 w.FS(), w.Net()

Inside a simulated World, code must not block any other way: a raw channel, sync.Mutex held across a wait, time.Sleep or real I/O escapes the scheduler. The simulator reports such escapes (it doesn't hang), and the dstlint analyzer finds them before running.

laws.text: The contract suite passes unchanged against the real World and the simulated one.
Select runs exactly one case, preferring ready ones.

Zero values of Chan, Mutex, RWMutex, WaitGroup and Once are ready to use.

systems.what: A `World` is built by worldhook from a scheduler, a machine, an epoch and an optional FS and Net. Without a scheduler it is the real World and calls go, time and the global generators directly. In a simulated World, goroutines are tasks of the World's machine and the clock is the epoch plus the scheduler's virtual time.

laws.detail: Since and Until are computed from Now, so they also follow the virtual clock.

laws.text: FS panics when the World has no filesystem; Net panics when it has no network.
In a simulated World, Go runs fn as a task on the caller's machine and is a scheduling point.

systems.purpose: A Go channel that both Worlds support, including non-blocking operations and range.
systems.what: A `Chan[T]` wraps a real Go channel, a receive-only channel from a library, or a channel simulated by sched. The zero Chan is a nil channel. Send, receive and close behave as the language defines them. TrySend and TryRecv replace a single-case select with a default.

interface.signature: func MakeChan[T any](w *World, size int) Chan[T]
interface.doc: Makes a channel of T with a buffer of the given size.

interface.name: RecvOnly
interface.doc: Adapts a real receive-only channel for the real World.

interface.doc: Sends v (c <- v).

interface.name: Chan.Recv
interface.doc: Receives a value and the ok flag (v, ok := <-c).

interface.name: Chan.Close
interface.doc: Closes the channel.

interface.name: Chan.TrySend
interface.doc: Sends without waiting; reports whether it sent.

interface.name: Chan.TryRecv
interface.signature: func (c Chan[T]) TryRecv() (v T, ok, received bool)
interface.doc: Receives without waiting; reports whether it received.

Close on the zero Chan panics; Send and Recv on it block forever.
TrySend and TryRecv on the zero Chan return false without waiting.
TryRecv reports received=true, ok=false when the channel is closed and drained.
laws.detail: received=false means nothing was ready.

laws.text: All stops once the channel is closed and drained, or when the loop breaks.
In a simulated World, TrySend and TryRecv are scheduling points.

systems.purpose: The select statement over Chan cases, in either World.
systems.what: `Select` takes cases built with OnRecv, OnSend, OnDone and Default. In the real World it calls reflect.Select. In a simulated World it yields first. It then checks the cases in an order the seed decides, and if none is ready and there is no Default, it registers a waiter on each non-nil channel and parks.

interface.doc: Runs exactly one case's function.

laws.detail: If all cases are on nil Chans and there is no Default, Select blocks forever. In a simulated World this is reported as a deadlock.

laws.text: A waiting OnSend case panics if its channel is closed before the send.
Passing a simulated Chan to Select in the real World panics.
In a simulated World, Select is always a scheduling point, even when a case is ready.

systems.name: Mutex
systems.title: Mutex
systems.purpose: sync.Mutex whose contended Lock waits through the scheduler.
systems.what: `Mutex` wraps a sync.Mutex. In a simulated World, a contended Lock parks on the scheduler and retries TryLock when woken. Unlock wakes one parked waiter. Outside a simulated task, Lock is the ordinary blocking Lock.

interface.name: Mutex.Lock
interface.doc: Acquires the lock.

interface.name: Mutex.TryLock
interface.doc: Acquires the lock only if it is free.

interface.name: Mutex.Unlock
interface.doc: Releases the lock.

laws.text: An uncontended Lock is not a scheduling point.
Unlock wakes a simulated goroutine parked in Lock, which then retries.

assumes.text: sync.Mutex provides mutual exclusion and panics on Unlock of an unlocked mutex.

systems.name: RWMutex
systems.title: Read-write mutex
systems.purpose: sync.RWMutex whose waits go through the scheduler, with writers getting priority.
systems.what: `RWMutex` wraps a sync.RWMutex and counts the simulated writers that are waiting. While any writer is waiting, new readers wait too. Every Unlock and RUnlock wakes all parked waiters, and each one retries.

interface.name: RWMutex.Lock
interface.doc: Acquires the write lock.

interface.name: RWMutex.Unlock
interface.doc: Releases the write lock.

interface.name: RWMutex.RLock
interface.doc: Acquires a read lock.

interface.name: RWMutex.RUnlock
interface.doc: Releases a read lock.

laws.text: While a writer waits in Lock, a new RLock waits too.
Unlock and RUnlock wake every parked simulated waiter to retry.

assumes.text: sync.RWMutex provides reader-writer exclusion.

systems.name: WaitGroup
systems.title: Wait group
systems.purpose: sync.WaitGroup whose Wait parks through the scheduler.
systems.what: `WaitGroup` keeps its own atomic counter next to a sync.WaitGroup. Simulated waiters park until the counter reaches zero. `Go` starts a counted goroutine on the World.

interface.name: WaitGroup.Add
interface.doc: Adds delta to the counter.

interface.name: WaitGroup.Done
interface.doc: Decrements the counter.

interface.name: WaitGroup.Go
interface.doc: Runs fn in a counted goroutine of w.

interface.name: WaitGroup.Wait
interface.doc: Waits until the counter is zero.

laws.text: Add that makes the counter negative panics.
Wait returns at once when the counter is zero.
When the counter reaches zero, every simulated goroutine parked in Wait wakes.
Go counts fn before starting it and calls Done when fn returns, even if fn panics.

systems.name: Once
systems.title: Once
systems.purpose: sync.Once whose concurrent callers wait through the World.
systems.what: `Once` is a dst Mutex plus an atomic done flag. Because the lock is a dst Mutex, callers that arrive while f is running park through the scheduler.

interface.name: Once.Do
interface.doc: Runs f if no earlier Do has run it.

laws.text: f runs at most once; a concurrent Do returns only after the first f returns.
If f panics, the Once still counts as done.

systems.what: A simulated Timer or Ticker schedules a scheduler event that sends to a channel with a buffer of one, or that spawns the AfterFunc goroutine. Each event is tied to the incarnation of the machine that created it. The real World wraps the time package.

interface.doc: Timer that fires once after d.

interface.name: World.After

interface.name: World.AfterFunc
interface.doc: Runs fn in its own goroutine after d.

interface.name: Timer.Stop
interface.doc: Stops the timer; reports whether it was active.

interface.name: Timer.Reset
interface.doc: Rearms the timer for d.

interface.name: World.NewTicker
interface.doc: Ticker that fires every d.

interface.name: Ticker.Stop
interface.doc: Stops the ticker.

interface.name: Ticker.Reset
interface.doc: Changes the period and restarts the ticker.

laws.text: After Timer.Stop returns, C never delivers a stale value.
laws.detail: If the timer had fired but nothing had received the value, Stop discards the value and returns true.

laws.text: Reset reports whether the timer was active and rearms it d after the current time.
A timer, ticker or AfterFunc never fires after its creating machine crashes.
AfterFunc runs fn in a new goroutine on the timer's machine.
A ticker drops ticks while its receiver is slow, and Stop discards any pending tick.
NewTicker panics on a non-positive interval.

assumes.text: sched.Timer.Stop reports whether the event was cancelled before it ran.

systems.name: dst.WithCancel
systems.title: Contexts
systems.purpose: Context cancellation and deadlines driven by the World instead of real timers.
systems.what: In a simulated World, contexts are `simCtx` values. Each has an inner standard cancel context, a simulated signal channel and an optional scheduler timer. Cancellation runs synchronously in the caller that cancels, with no goroutines. `Done` and `AfterDone` let World code wait on any context that dst can follow.

interface.doc: Derives a context that can be cancelled.

interface.name: WithTimeout
interface.signature: func WithTimeout(w *World, parent context.Context, d time.Duration) (context.Context, context.CancelFunc)
interface.doc: Derives a context that is done after d on the World's clock.

interface.name: WithDeadline
interface.signature: func WithDeadline(w *World, parent context.Context, deadline time.Time) (context.Context, context.CancelFunc)
interface.doc: Derives a context that is done at the deadline.

interface.name: Done
interface.doc: The context's done signal as a Chan.

interface.name: AfterDone
interface.signature: func AfterDone(ctx context.Context, f func()) (stop func() bool)
interface.doc: Runs f once the context is done; returns a stop function.

laws.text: Cancelling a simulated context cancels its descendants synchronously, in creation order.
The first cancellation sets Err; later cancels and deadlines leave it unchanged.
WithDeadline with a deadline already past returns a context done with DeadlineExceeded.
Under a parent whose deadline is no later, WithDeadline reports and obeys the parent's deadline.
In a simulated World, deriving from, Done or AfterDone on a foreign cancellable context panics.
laws.detail: Contexts with no Done channel, and standard contexts below a dst context, are allowed.

laws.text: A standard child of a simulated context whose deadline passed reports Canceled, with cause DeadlineExceeded.

systems.name: dstgrpc
systems.title: gRPC over World
systems.purpose: Runs gRPC services and clients in a World.
systems.what:
Your generated code and service implementations stay unchanged:

s := dstgrpc.NewServer(w)              // instead of grpc.NewServer() pb.RegisterFooServer(s, impl)          // unchanged go s.Serve(ln)                         // ln from w.Net().Listen

In the real World these are grpc-go's server and client. In a simulated World, Server implements grpc.ServiceRegistrar and the client implements grpc.ClientConnInterface over the World's network with a compact framing (one connection per call), so faults, latency and deadlines follow the seed and the World's clock. Unary and streaming calls, metadata (headers and trailers), status codes and interceptors are supported; status details are not carried.

laws.text: The same generated code and implementation work in both Worlds: unary and streaming calls, status codes, metadata.
A call's deadline reaches the server's context and ends the call with DeadlineExceeded, even if the server never answers.
Unary and stream interceptors wrap every call, on both sides.
Interceptors installed by several options run in option order, the first outermost.

Each call reads a call header (method, timeout, metadata), builds a context bounded by the World's clock, sends the request to the generated handler through the interceptors, and writes back a header, any reply messages and a trailer with the status. Headers and trailers set through grpc.SetHeader, SendHeader and SetTrailer reach the client.

A client hanging up during a unary call cancels the handler's context.
laws.detail: After the request is decoded, a watcher reads the connection and cancels the context on error or EOF.

laws.text: A stream's RecvMsg returns io.EOF after CloseSend, and Canceled if the client went away.
SetHeader after the header has been sent returns an error.

After Stop, Serve returns the listener's error.

Ending the call's context stops a blocked call, even if the server is silent.

systems.name: dstgrpc.framer
systems.title: Wire framing
systems.purpose: Encodes calls as typed, length-prefixed frames on one connection.
systems.what: Each frame is a type byte, a 4-byte big-endian length and a payload. The types are call header, message and close-send from the client, and header and trailer from the server. Metadata and strings are length-prefixed, and messages are encoded with deterministic protobuf marshalling, so a seed always produces the same bytes on the wire.

assumes.text: World connections deliver written bytes in order, without duplication.

systems.name: dstlint

systems.what:
A package opts in with a comment in any of its files:

//dst:simulated

A line can be excused with a comment on it or the line above:

mu.Lock() //dst:ok guards a cache no goroutine waits on

Packages without //dst:simulated aren't reported.
A //dst:ok comment on or above a line suppresses its report.
One //dst:simulated comment in any file opts in every file of the package.
laws.detail: The comment must be exactly `//dst:simulated` after trimming spaces. Trailing text or a block comment does not opt the package in.

laws.text: Method calls are never reported by name; only package-level functions match the function table.

systems.name: dsttest
systems.title: Simulation test runner
systems.purpose: Runs deterministic simulation tests: it sweeps seeds, and for each one builds a simulated World of machines, injects faults, checks invariants, and reports failures with a command that replays them exactly.
systems.what:
func TestStore(t *testing.T) { dsttest.Run(t, dsttest.Options{Seeds: 500, Faults: dsttest.AllFaults}, func(h *dsttest.Harness) { for _, name := range []string{"db1", "db2", "db3"} { h.Machine(name, func(w *dst.World) { store.Serve(w, name) }) } h.Go(func(w *dst.World) { workload(w, h) })     // clients, on a machine that never fails h.Always("one leader", checkLeaders)            // after every step h.Final("converged", checkConverged)            // after recovery }) }

The setup function runs once per seed, possibly in parallel with other seeds: keep every piece of state the run uses inside it.

Each seed runs in phases. During the fault phase the runner crashes and restarts machines, partitions the network and lets disks lose unsynced data, at rates chosen per seed (swarm testing: some seeds turn whole fault classes off). During the recovery phase every machine is back and the network is whole: a correct system must recover. Then the Final checks run. A failing seed prints:

go test -run '^TestStore$' -dst.seed=2891 -dst.v

which reruns exactly that seed with an event log.

systems.name: dedupe
systems.title: Exactly-once dedupe
systems.purpose: Is exactly-once processing over at-least-once delivery: a producer retries each message until it is acknowledged, and a consumer applies each message once however often it arrives, across its own crashes.
systems.what:
Ordinary Go (goroutines, a mutex, TCP, files) written against a dst.World.

The consumer keeps one write-ahead log of applied message IDs: applying a message and remembering that it was applied are the same durable record, so no crash can separate them.

Bugs plants known mistakes; the test shows the simulator catches each.

interface.name: Consumer.Apply
interface.doc: Applies a message ID unless it was already applied.

interface.name: Consumer.Serve
interface.doc: Accepts producers; acknowledges each line's ID once applied.

interface.name: EffectsLog
interface.doc: File name of the log of applied IDs.

interface.name: Bugs
interface.doc: Switches that plant known consumer mistakes.

laws.text: Every message the producer delivers is applied exactly once, under crashes, partitions, resets and power loss.
Once faults stop, every message is acknowledged.
The wire protocol is one ID per line, answered with "ok <id>".
laws.detail: Both the producer and the consumer rely on this framing. An ID that contains a newline cannot be delivered.

systems.name: dedupe.Consumer
systems.title: Consumer
systems.purpose: Applies each message ID once, durably, and acknowledges it over TCP.
systems.what: The consumer owns the `EffectsLog` write-ahead log. Each record in it is an applied message ID, and an in-memory seen set is rebuilt from that log when the consumer starts. `Apply` takes a mutex, skips IDs already seen, and otherwise appends the ID to the log before marking it seen. `Serve` handles producer connections, one goroutine per connection, and acknowledges each ID only after it has been applied. Durability itself is left to the `wal` package.

interface.name: NewConsumer
interface.doc: Opens EffectsLog and rebuilds the seen set from it.

interface.name: Consumer.Apply
interface.doc: Applies a message ID unless it was already applied.

interface.name: Consumer.Serve
interface.doc: Serves producers on a listener until Accept fails.

interface.name: EffectsLog
interface.doc: File name of the log of applied IDs, in order.

interface.name: Bugs
interface.doc: Switches that plant known consumer mistakes.

laws.text: Apply of an already-applied ID returns nil and appends nothing.
After NewConsumer, every ID recorded in EffectsLog counts as already applied.
laws.detail: This holds with no Bugs set: the seen set is rebuilt from the effects records themselves.

laws.text: EffectsLog holds applied IDs in apply order, each at most once.
Apply that returns an error leaves the ID unapplied in memory, so a retry may apply it.
Serve sends "ok <id>" only after Apply of that ID returned nil.
laws.detail: If Apply fails, the connection is closed without an acknowledgement, so the producer retries.

laws.text: Serve returns only when Accept fails, returning that error.

assumes.text: wal.Log.Append returns only after the record is durable.
wal.Open recovers every record whose Append succeeded, in append order.
dst.Mutex gives mutual exclusion among World goroutines.

systems.name: dedupe.Deliver
systems.title: Producer
systems.purpose: Delivers a message ID at least once, retrying until it is acknowledged.
systems.what: `Deliver` is the at-least-once side. Each attempt dials the consumer, sends the ID as one line and waits for the matching "ok <id>" reply, all within a timeout. Failed attempts are retried after an exponential backoff with random jitter, timed and seeded through the World. Removing duplicates is left to the consumer.

interface.name: Deliver
interface.doc: Sends an ID until acknowledged, retrying with backoff.

laws.text: Deliver returns only after reading exactly "ok <id>" for its own ID.
laws.detail: A reply for some other ID, or any read error, counts as a failed attempt.

laws.text: Each attempt, including dial, write and read, ends within 300ms of World time.

systems.name: lease
systems.title: Lease service
systems.purpose: Is a lock service with leases: a server grants one client at a time the right to act for a limited time, and clients renew it.
systems.what:
Ordinary Go (goroutines, TCP, timers) written against a dst.World.

Safety rests on time: a client may act only until its lease ends, and the server grants the lease to someone else only after it ended. Both sides must measure conservatively:

- the client counts its lease from when it sent the request (the server granted it later, so it expires later there); - a client that can't renew stops acting when its lease ends; - a restarted server, which forgot its grants, waits one lease length before granting anything.

Bugs plants the classic mistakes; the test shows the simulator catches each.

interface.name: TTL
interface.doc: Length of every lease.

interface.name: Bugs
interface.doc: Switches that plant classic lease mistakes.

interface.name: Server.Serve
interface.doc: Answers acquire/release requests on a listener.

interface.name: Client.Run
interface.doc: Acquires and renews the lease forever.

interface.name: Client.Holds

laws.text: At no moment do two live clients believe they hold the lease, under crashes, partitions and latency spikes.
Once faults stop, some client gets the lease.
With all Bugs off, every lease the server grants outlasts the client's own view of it.
laws.detail: The client counts from before it sent the request and the server from when it granted, so the server's expiry is always later.

assumes.text: Every party's `World.Now` advances at the same rate and never goes backwards.
assumes.detail: Both sides compare times measured on their own clocks, each counted over TTL.

systems.what: Keeps the current holder and its expiry in memory, protected by a `dst.Mutex`. `Serve` accepts connections and answers one line per connection: `acquire <client>` or `release <client>`. Because a restarted server has forgotten its grants, it refuses all grants for one TTL after it starts. It leaves keeping track of time on the client side to the client.

Acquire by the current holder renews it to TTL from now.
laws.detail: This is how renewal works: no separate renew command.

laws.text: Release by anyone other than the holder leaves the lease in place.
laws.detail: Release always answers "ok".

Unknown commands get "error" and leave state unchanged.
Serve returns only when Accept fails, and returns that error.

systems.title: Lease client
systems.purpose: Acquires and renews the lease and tracks when its lease ends.
systems.what: A named client that loops forever. It sends `acquire`, and on a grant it sets `End` to TTL from the moment it sent the request. While it holds the lease it works for TTL/3 and then renews. Otherwise it waits a random time below TTL. `Holds` compares the World's clock with `End`. Every request uses the World's network with a deadline of TTL/4.

systems.name: twophase
systems.title: Two-phase commit
systems.purpose: Is two-phase commit: a coordinator moves money between accounts held by two participants, atomically, despite crashes of any of them and a network that loses, delays and partitions.
systems.what:
Ordinary Go (goroutines, a mutex, TCP, files) written against a dst.World.

Each participant holds one account. A transfer is a transaction with a delta for each participant. The coordinator logs "begin", asks both to prepare, logs its decision, and tells them. A participant that votes yes has first logged the prepared delta, so it can still commit after a crash; while in doubt it holds its lock and asks the coordinator. A restarted coordinator aborts every transaction it began but didn't decide (presumed abort).

Bugs plants the classic mistakes; the test shows the simulator catches each.

systems.name: wal
systems.title: Write-ahead log
systems.purpose: Is a write-ahead log: an append-only file of checksummed records that survives crashes.
systems.what:
It is ordinary Go written against a dst.World's filesystem, and an example of what deterministic simulation finds in storage code.

A record is a 4-byte length, a 4-byte CRC-32 of the data, and the data. Append returns only once the record is durable. Open recovers: it reads records until the first incomplete or corrupt one (a write torn by a crash), truncates the file there, and continues after it.

Bugs plants known mistakes; the test shows the simulator catches each.

After a crash, Open returns a prefix of the appended records.
laws.detail: It may lack only unacknowledged ones at the end: never garbage, never a gap.

laws.text: The same code runs on the real filesystem.
Append's returned indexes are consecutive and continue after the recovered records.
laws.detail: The first Append after Open returns len(Records()) as it was after recovery.

laws.text: Records returns the recovered records followed by each successful Append's data, in order.
laws.detail: Open on a file that doesn't exist yet gives an empty Records.

laws.text: An Append that returns an error adds nothing to Records.
Open sets TornTail exactly when bytes follow the last intact record.
laws.detail: A record is intact when its full length is present and its CRC-32 matches. Parsing stops at the first record that isn't.

laws.text: After Open finds a torn tail, the file holds only the intact records.
laws.detail: This holds with the zero Bugs value. Open truncates and fsyncs before it returns, so Read afterwards sees the same records Open did.

laws.text: Read never modifies the log file.
With the zero Bugs value, the log behaves correctly.

systems.title: Worker pool
systems.purpose: Runs a function over many inputs with a bounded number of goroutines, returning results in order, or the first error after stopping the rest.
systems.what:
It is plain concurrent Go (goroutines, channels, a WaitGroup, a context) migrated to a dst.World by mechanical substitution:

go f()                 -> w.Go(f) make(chan T, n)        -> dst.MakeChan[T](w, n) ch <- v / <-ch         -> ch.Send(v) / ch.Recv() for v := range ch      -> for v := range ch.All() select { ... }         -> dst.Select(w, dst.OnRecv(...), dst.OnDone(ctx, ...)) sync.WaitGroup         -> dst.WaitGroup context.WithCancel     -> dst.WithCancel

Bugs plants common Go concurrency mistakes; the test shows the simulator catches each.

interface.name: Bugs
interface.doc: Switches that make Map commit a classic concurrency mistake.

laws.text: Map returns every result in input order, or the first error, under every interleaving the seeds explore.
Map returns only after every goroutine it started has finished, also on error.
After Map sees the first error it dispatches no further inputs to fn.
laws.detail: Cancelling the derived context stops the producer. Inputs that workers already hold still finish and their results are drained.

laws.text: The context fn receives is cancelled at the first error and when Map returns.
Map calls fn at most once per input.
laws.detail: Each index goes onto the jobs channel once, and exactly one worker receives it.

laws.text: When Map returns an error, the result slice is nil, never partial.
Cancelling the caller's context stops dispatch without making Map return an error.
laws.detail: If the caller cancels and no fn call fails, Map returns a nil error. Inputs that were never dispatched keep the value 0 in the result slice.

laws.text: A zero Bugs value gives the correct Map; each true field plants one mistake.

Chan.All ends once the channel is closed and drained.
dst.WaitGroup.Wait returns only after every Add is matched by Done.

systems.name: sched
systems.title: Simulation scheduler
systems.purpose: Is the deterministic engine under the simulated World: a baton scheduler for goroutines, a virtual clock with timers, wait queues, and machines (groups of goroutines that crash together).
systems.what: Every simulated goroutine (a Task) is a real goroutine, but only one runs at a time. It holds the baton until it reaches a scheduling point (a World operation), where it hands the baton back and the seed picks which runnable task goes next. When none is runnable, the clock jumps to the next timer. Nothing else decides the order, so a seed replays exactly.

systems.name: simfs
systems.title: Simulated disk
systems.purpose: Is a simulated disk for one machine: an in-memory filesystem with os semantics, behind a page cache that a crash empties the way real kernels and disks may.
systems.what:
It is adversarial but legal. Live operations behave exactly like os (the contract suite runs against both). What survives a crash is anything POSIX and real journaling filesystems allow, chosen by the seed:

- Data written to a file is durable only after the file's Sync. - Directory changes (create, mkdir, rename, remove) form one ordered journal: a crash keeps a prefix of the unsynced ones, and a Sync of a directory makes the journal durable up to that directory's last change. A rename is atomic. - By default each file's unsynced writes survive independently of other files' (as on ext4 data=writeback or XFS), and a file's Sync covers its own data only. With Ordered, everything is one queue in issue order and any Sync commits everything before it, like a journal commit on ext4's default data=ordered. - The first lost write of a file may survive in part (torn). - Power can fail inside a Write, Sync or directory operation. - Open files go stale after a crash.

systems.name: simnet
systems.title: Simulated network
systems.purpose: Is a simulated network between machines: TCP-like connections with seeded latency, partitions and resets, implementing net.Listener and net.Conn so code written against the net package runs on it.
systems.what:
Its model of TCP:

- Bytes on a connection arrive in order, exactly once, each write after a seeded latency. - A partition stalls a connection (like TCP retransmitting): nothing crosses it, and after Heal everything held arrives, in order. - A crashed machine is silent (power loss sends nothing): its peers' reads wait, until their deadlines or until the machine restarts and answers their next packet with a reset. - Data sent to a closed connection is answered with a reset, which arrives after anything sent before it and discards what the receiver hasn't read yet (so closing with unread input can destroy a response in flight, as RFC 7230 §6.6 warns). - Dialing an address with no listener is refused; dialing across a partition waits for Heal or the deadline. - ResetProb resets connections at random, as middleboxes and kernels do.

Addresses are "machine:port"; "localhost" is the dialing machine.

It also records the incarnation of the machine that owns it, so a peer's traffic arriving after that machine restarts is answered with a reset.

A reset is queued behind data the resetting end already sent.

systems.purpose: Check that channels, select, timers, locks, contexts and rand behave like Go.

Time checks measure in World time (`w.Now`, `w.Since`), so they hold under virtual time as well as real time.

laws.text: Fails a World whose buffered Chan is not FIFO or whose Close semantics differ from Go's.
laws.detail: After Close, values already buffered can still be received, and a drained receive returns (0, false). Send or Close on a closed channel panics with Go's exact messages. A blocked receiver is woken with ok=false.

laws.text: Fails a Select that runs Default while a case is ready, or always picks the same ready case.
laws.detail: Over 200 selects with both cases ready, both must be chosen at least once. Nil channels must never be ready.

laws.text: Fails timers that fire out of deadline order, or Stop that fails to prevent a fire.
laws.detail: This covers stopped timers, stopped AfterFuncs and stopped tickers. Reset must re-arm a timer that was stopped.

laws.text: Fails a Mutex or RWMutex that lets a writer overlap anyone, or never lets readers overlap.
Fails Once.Do if f runs more than once or Do returns before f finishes.
Fails World contexts whose cancel or timeout doesn't reach their children, standard-library children included.

laws.text: Fails an FS whose missing-path and existing-path errors don't match fs.ErrNotExist and fs.ErrExist.
laws.detail: Covered calls: Open, Mkdir, Rename and Remove of missing paths, O_EXCL on an existing file, and Mkdir of an existing directory.

laws.text: Fails an FS where writes past the end or Truncate growth don't zero-fill the gap.
Fails an FS where Rename doesn't atomically replace its target and drop the old name.
Fails an FS where an open file stops being readable after Remove.
Fails an FS that allows a path outside its root, such as "../escape".
Fails an FS where a closed handle can write or close again without an error.
laws.detail: Write after Close must return fs.ErrClosed.

laws.text: Fails an FS where FS.ReadDir isn't sorted by name, or Remove deletes a non-empty directory.
laws.detail: File.ReadDir order is allowed to be unspecified. RemoveAll of a missing path must succeed.

systems.name: worldtest.NetChecks
systems.title: Network checks
systems.purpose: Check that w.Net() behaves like loopback TCP.
systems.what: NetChecks runs against `w.Net()` with a listener on localhost:0. It asserts TCP-like stream semantics: echo, delivery in order, refused dials, read deadlines measured in World time, and EOF after the peer closes.

interface.name: NetChecks
interface.doc: Network contract checks over a localhost TCP listener.

laws.text: Fails a Net whose stream loses, reorders or duplicates the bytes written.
Fails a Net where Dial to a closed listener succeeds, or where Accept after Close isn't net.ErrClosed.
Fails a Net where a read past its deadline isn't a net.Error with Timeout() true.
laws.detail: The deadline is set from w.Now(), so it is World time.

laws.text: Fails a Net where reading after the peer closes isn't io.EOF, or writing after Close succeeds.

systems.name: realworld
systems.title: Production World
systems.purpose: Provides the production World: real goroutines, the real clock, real randomness, the operating system's files and network.
systems.what: Every operation is the plain Go one, so code written against a *dst.World runs in production with negligible overhead.

interface.name: Options
interface.doc: Configures the real World; Dir roots the filesystem.

interface.name: osFS.OpenFile
interface.signature: func (f *osFS) OpenFile(name string, flag int, perm fs.FileMode) (dst.File, error)
interface.doc: Opens a file under the root, reached via w.FS().

interface.name: osNet.Dial
interface.doc: Dials with the plain net package, via w.Net().

interface.name: osNet.Listen
interface.doc: Listens with the plain net package, via w.Net().

laws.text: Every World operation behaves as the plain Go operation it replaces (the contract suite passes).
New never fails, even when Options.Dir does not exist.
laws.detail: The root directory is opened lazily on the first w.FS() call, so a bad Dir surfaces as an FS error, not at construction.

laws.text: Network calls are not confined: Listen and Dial reach any address the OS allows.

assumes.text: worldhook.NewWorld with a Spec returns a *dst.World using real goroutines and clock.
assumes.detail: The type assertion in New panics otherwise.

systems.name: realworld.osFS
systems.title: Rooted filesystem
systems.purpose: Operating system filesystem confined to one directory via os.Root.
systems.what: `osFS` implements `dst.FS` over an `os.Root` opened once, on first use, at the configured directory (the current directory when empty). Every operation resolves names relative to that root, so code cannot reach files outside it. Durability and crash behaviour are whatever the OS provides.

interface.name: osFS.OpenFile
interface.signature: func (f *osFS) OpenFile(name string, flag int, perm fs.FileMode) (dst.File, error)
interface.doc: Opens or creates a file relative to the root.

interface.name: osFS.Mkdir
interface.signature: func (f *osFS) Mkdir(name string, perm fs.FileMode) error
interface.doc: Creates one directory under the root.

interface.name: osFS.MkdirAll
interface.signature: func (f *osFS) MkdirAll(name string, perm fs.FileMode) error
interface.doc: Creates a directory path under the root.

interface.name: osFS.Remove
interface.doc: Removes a file or empty directory under the root.

interface.name: osFS.RemoveAll
interface.doc: Removes a tree under the root.

interface.name: osFS.Rename
interface.doc: Renames within the root.

interface.name: osFS.Stat
interface.doc: Describes a name under the root.

interface.name: osFS.ReadDir
interface.doc: Lists a directory under the root, sorted by name.

laws.text: No FS call can read or change a name outside Options.Dir.
laws.detail: Absolute paths, `..` and escaping symlinks are rejected with an error.

laws.text: An empty Options.Dir roots the FS at the current directory.
If the root cannot be opened, every FS call returns that same error.
laws.detail: The root is opened once; the failure is cached, not retried.

laws.text: A failed OpenFile returns a nil dst.File, never a typed-nil *os.File.

assumes.text: os.Root rejects names that resolve outside its directory.
